paras: The attempted lynching of Bert Hazelock was an assault by a white crowd on a Black man in Albany, New York, on the afternoon of August 2, 1903, after he was accused of cutting a white man with a razor during a street fight. The crowd chased him through the streets, and a thrown paving stone broke his arm before he took refuge in a house that the crowd surrounded. A policeman, John Begley, held the crowd back with a drawn revolver until other officers arrived and took Hazelock to the station house. New York and Washington papers reported it the next day as an attempted lynching, and weekly news digests repeated it.

The trouble began on Third street on Arbor Hill, where two Black men were fighting. A white man named Scharff, given as John Scharff in the Herald and in a Baltimore Sun dispatch, tried to separate them. According to the New York Sun, which spelled the name "Hazzelock," Hazelock told Scharff to attend to his own business, the two fought, and Hazelock stabbed Scharff in the back with a razor. The other dispatch said only that he slashed Scharff with a razor; the Sun called the cut "only skin deep."

A crowd of white men drawn by the brawl rushed at Hazelock, who ran down Third street; the Sun said the crowd was headed by Scharff. Its members shouted "Lynch the nigger!" and, in the Herald's version, "Hang him!" Stones, bricks and other missiles were thrown after him, and a paving stone broke his arm and knocked him down. The New York Sun did not mention the injury.

Hazelock got to his feet and kept running, and by the Herald's count the crowd grew from about fifty men to two hundred. He ran into a house on Second street near Swan street, frightening the women who lived there, and bolted the door. The crowd surrounded the house and, in the Sun's account, demanded his surrender.

Officer John Begley, of the Third precinct according to the Baltimore Sun dispatch, arrived and went into the house to arrest Hazelock. When he brought his prisoner out, several men rushed forward to seize him, and Begley drew his revolver and kept them back until other policemen arrived. The officers escorted Hazelock to the station house, where he was locked up.
No report of a charge or trial for Hazelock, or of arrests in the crowd, was found.

The story reached readers through two separately written dispatches, both datelined Albany on August 2. The New York Sun headlined its version "Albany Mob Chases Negro" and credited "the pluck of Patrolman Begley" for the outcome. The New York Herald printed a special despatch headed "Albany Mob Would Lynch a Negro," which stated plainly that "an attempt was made to lynch" Hazelock. A nearly identical Baltimore Sun dispatch ran the same day in the Washington Evening Star ("Attempt Made to Lynch Black Who Cut Peacemaker") and the Alexandria Gazette.

Both versions called Hazelock "the negro," printed the crowd's slur, and treated the razor attack as settled, with no account from Hazelock or Black witnesses. The Baltimore Sun text cast Scharff as a "peacemaker" and Hazelock as "trembling with fear," and set the scene in "the quiet old city of Albany."

Farther afield, the Arizona Republican reprinted the Sun's text on August 10 under the same headline but with the dateline "Aug. 9." Wisconsin weeklies' "News of the World" digests reduced the episode to a single sentence, reporting that the lynching "was prevented by the police after a riot, in which stones and bricks were thrown." No Black-press account of the episode was found.

The Herald and Baltimore Sun texts counted fifty men growing to two hundred, while the New York Sun spoke of "hundreds" and "nearly a thousand people." The house stood on Second street in the New York papers but on "2d avenue" or "Second avenue" in the Baltimore Sun text, in each case near Swan street. The Arizona Republican's "Aug. 9" dateline appears to be a reprint error, since its text matches the Sun's August 2 dispatch word for word.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bert Hazelock
bases: A white crowd chased Hazelock crying 'Lynch the nigger!' and 'Hang him!', broke his arm with a stone and besieged the house where he hid, and the Herald and Baltimore Sun dispatch called it an attempt to lynch him (A2, A3); he survived, so it is an attempted lynching.

A crowd of fifty to two hundred or more acting without authority tried to lynch Hazelock over his alleged razor attack on a white man (A1, A2, A3), but police took him to the station house alive, so no one was killed (A2, A3).

Two independently written dispatches, the New York Sun's (A1) and the Herald/Baltimore Sun text (A2, A3), agree on the razor cut, the chase, the surrounded house on Second street and Begley's rescue with a revolver.

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: Hazzelock told Scharff to mind his own business, the two fought and he stabbed Scharff with a glancing, skin-deep razor cut; a crowd headed by Scharff that grew to hundreds chased him to a house, where Begley held it off with a revolver.

accounts.label: Herald / Baltimore Sun special dispatch
accounts.gist: Hazelock slashed Scharff, a peacemaker, with a razor; fifty white men, growing to two hundred, chased him crying 'Lynch the nigger!', a paving stone broke his arm, and Begley drew his revolver when men rushed to seize him from custody.

accounts.label: News digest
accounts.gist: One sentence: the lynching was prevented by the police after a riot with stones and bricks.

framing.detail: The Sun's 'Albany Mob Chases Negro' credited 'the pluck of Patrolman Begley' and called the crowd a would-be mob in 'staid old Albany', while treating the stabbing as fact.

Herald ('Albany Mob Would Lynch a Negro') and Baltimore Sun text ('Attempt Made to Lynch Black Who Cut Peacemaker') reported the attempt plainly, printed the crowd's slur, and cast Scharff as 'peacemaker'.
Alexandria Gazette and Arizona Republican reprinted the two dispatches; Wisconsin weekly digests reduced it to one sentence.
